title: Roman Numeral Converter
tagline: An early two-way Roman numeral converter with its own validity check
summary: I wrote this on a Raspberry Pi before I even knew about while loops. It converts Roman numerals into regular numbers, checks whether the input is valid, and uses a separate conversion routine for the other direction. Looking back at it is a fun snapshot of how I solved problems before I knew the normal tools for solving them.

overview.what: A Python program that converts Roman numerals to regular numbers and back, and checks whether a Roman numeral is written correctly.
overview.why: It was one of the first things I wrote on my Raspberry Pi, before I even knew about while loops.
overview.did: I came up with my own way to check the input: turn it into a number, turn that back into a Roman numeral, and see if it matches what you typed.
overview.result: It works, and it's a fun snapshot of how I solved problems before I knew the normal tools for them. You can try it right on this page.

sections.heading: A strange but useful validator
body: The program reads your Roman numeral, turns the answer back into a properly written Roman numeral, and compares the two. If they don't match, it rejects things like IIII and suggests IV instead.

sections.heading: How the two directions work
body: Reading a Roman numeral goes left to right. A symbol gets added when it's at least as big as the one after it, and subtracted when a bigger one comes next. That's why VI is 5 + 1, but IV is -1 + 5.

Writing one goes the other way. The converter keeps taking the biggest symbol or pair, like CM or IV, that fits into the number, adds it, and keeps going with what's left. You can try it in the converter above.
